<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Whenever a family indexed by \(\varepsilon\) is called equicoercive, the assertion is
sequential at the singular scale: for every \(\varepsilon_n\downarrow0\), every
sequence with uniformly bounded energy has a subsequence converging in the
stated topology.  No uniform assertion for \(\varepsilon\) bounded away from zero is
intended.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:cell-regularity}
For every \(q\in\mathcal A\), the map
\((x,n)\mapsto e(x,n;q)\) is continuous on
\(\Omega\times\mathbb S^{d-1}\).  The cell density \(\gamma\) is jointly upper
semicontinuous, even in \(n\), and locally uniformly bounded.  More precisely,
for every compact \(K\Subset\Omega\),
\[
 0\le\gamma(x,n)\le \frac14\int_{\mathbb R^d}J(x,Z)|Z\cdot n|\,\mathrm d Z
 \le \frac{R_JM_K}{4}
\]
for \((x,n)\in K\times\mathbb S^{d-1}\).
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Fix \(q\in\mathcal A\) and write
\[
 I_q(a):=\int_\mathbb R|q(s)-q(s-a)|^2\,\mathrm d s.
\]
Write \(q=q_0+w\), where
\(q_0=\mathbf 1_{(0,\infty)}\) and \(w\in L^2(\mathbb R)\) has compact support.  The map
\(a\mapsto q_0-q_0(\cdot-a)\) is continuous into \(L^2(\mathbb R)\), because the
squared distance between the increments at \(a\) and \(b\) is \(|a-b|\).
Translation continuity in \(L^2(\mathbb R)\) gives the same conclusion for
\(w-w(\cdot-a)\).  Hence
\(a\mapsto q-q(\cdot-a)\) is \(L^2\)-continuous and \(I_q\) is continuous.
On \([-R_J,R_J]\) it is bounded by a constant depending only on \(q\) and
\(R_J\).  Thus
\[
 e(x,n;q)=\int_\mathbb R W(q(s))\,\mathrm d s
 +\frac14\int_{B_{R_J}}J(x,Z)I_q(Z\cdot n)\,\mathrm d Z.
\]
If \((x_k,n_k)\to(x,n)\), the part caused by \(x_k\to x\) tends to zero by
the \(L^1\)-continuity in \eqref{eq:l1-cont}; the part caused by
\(n_k\to n\) tends to zero by dominated convergence.  Hence the fixed-profile
cost is continuous.  Its infimum over \(q\) is upper semicontinuous.

Evenness follows by \(Z\mapsto-Z\) and \eqref{eq:even}.  Finally use the step
profile \(q_0=\mathbf 1_{(0,\infty)}\).  Its potential cost vanishes, while the set
of \(s\) for which \(q_0(s)\ne q_0(s-Z\cdot n)\) has length
\(|Z\cdot n|\).  This proves the displayed bound.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Let \(\zeta\in C_c(\Omega)\), \(\zeta\ge0\), and let \(E\subset\Omega\) have
finite perimeter in a neighbourhood of \(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\).  Then there exist
\(u_\varepsilon:\mathbb R^d\to[0,1]\) such that
\(u_\varepsilon\to\mathbf 1_E\) in \(L^1_{\rm loc}(\Omega)\) and
\[
 \limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_\varepsilon;\zeta)
 \le
 \int_{\partial^*E}\zeta(x)\gamma(x,\nu_E(x))
 \,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x).
\]
Here \(\nu_E=D\mathbf 1_E/|D\mathbf 1_E|\) is the normal from the zero phase to the
one phase.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:allocation}
Let \(F\) be a bounded relatively open polyhedral subset of an affine
hyperplane with unit normal \(n\), compactly contained in \(\Omega\).  For
every \(\eta>0\), there are finitely many pairwise disjoint relatively open
polyhedral sets \(B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_N\subset F\), covering \(F\) up to an
\(\mathcal H^{d-1}\)-null set, and profiles \(q_0,q_1,\ldots,q_N\in\mathcal A\)
such that \(q_0=\mathbf 1_{(0,\infty)}\) and
\[
 \sum_{a=0}^N\int_{B_a}\zeta(x)e(x,n;q_a)\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x)
 \le
 \int_F\zeta(x)\gamma(x,n)\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x)+\eta.
 \label{eq:allocation}
\]
The union of the relative boundaries of the \(B_a\)'s is a finite
codimension-two polyhedral complex.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Set \(f(x)=\zeta(x)\gamma(x,n)\) on \(F\).  Lemma
\ref{lem:cell-regularity} makes \(f\) bounded and measurable.  Let \(G\subset
F\) be the full-measure set of its Lebesgue points.  Fix a small
\(\delta>0\).  For each \(x\in G\), choose \(q_x\in\mathcal A\) with
\[
 e(x,n;q_x)\le\gamma(x,n)+\delta.
\]
The function \(g_x(y):=\zeta(y)e(y,n;q_x)\) is continuous at \(x\) by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cell-regularity}.  Hence, for all sufficiently small cubes
\(Q\Subset F\), centred at \(x\) and with axes fixed in the hyperplane,
\[
 \int_Q g_x\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}
 \le \int_Q f\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}+C\delta\mathcal H^{d-1}(Q),
 \label{eq:local-cube}
\]
where \(C\) depends only on \(\|\zeta\|_\infty\).  Indeed, after division by
\(\mathcal H^{d-1}(Q)\), the two sides converge respectively to \(g_x(x)\) and
\(f(x)\).

The cubes satisfying \eqref{eq:local-cube}, with arbitrarily small side
length, form a Vitali cover of \(G\).  Select a pairwise disjoint countable
subfamily \((Q_a)_{a\ge1}\) covering \(F\) up to a null set.  Let
\[
 C_0:=\sup_{y\in F}e(y,n;q_0)<\infty,
\]
which follows from the step-profile estimate in
Lemma~\ref{lem:cell-regularity}.  Choose \(N\) so large that
\[
 \mathcal H^{d-1}\left(F\setminus\bigcup_{a=1}^NQ_a\right)
 \le \frac{\delta}{1+C_0\|\zeta\|_\infty}.
\]
Set \(B_a=Q_a\) and \(q_a=q_{x_a}\) for \(1\le a\le N\), where \(x_a\) is
the centre selected with \(Q_a\), and decompose the polyhedral remainder
\(F\setminus\bigcup_{a=1}^N\overline{Q_a}\) into its finitely many relatively
  open polyhedral components, all carrying the same profile \(q_0\); their union
  is denoted by \(B_0\).  Summing \eqref{eq:local-cube} and using the uniform
  bound on the remainder gives, with
  \(R_N:=F\setminus\bigcup_{a=1}^N\overline{Q_a}\),
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
   \sum_{a=0}^N\int_{B_a}\zeta e(\cdot,n;q_a)\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}
   &\le \int_{\cup_{a=1}^NQ_a}f\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}
      +C\delta\mathcal H^{d-1}(F)\\
   &\quad+C_0\|\zeta\|_\infty\mathcal H^{d-1}(R_N)\\
   &\le \int_F f\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}+C_F\delta.
  \end{aligned}
  \]
Choose \(\delta\) so that \(C_F\delta\le\eta\).  A finite family of
polyhedral boundaries has a finite codimension-two union, proving the last
claim.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:collar}
Let \(S\) be a finite codimension-two polyhedral complex in a neighbourhood
of \(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\), and let
\[
 \varepsilon\ll\ell_\varepsilon\downarrow0,
 \qquad \frac{\ell_\varepsilon^2}{\varepsilon}\to0.
\]
If two functions \(u_\varepsilon,v_\varepsilon:\mathbb R^d\to[0,1]\) agree outside
\(N_{\ell_\varepsilon}(S)\), then
\[
 |\mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_\varepsilon;\zeta)
  -\mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(v_\varepsilon;\zeta)|=o(1).
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Choose a compact \(K\Subset\Omega\) containing a fixed neighbourhood of
\(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\).  In the interaction difference, make for each \(Z\) the
change of variables \(m=x-\theta\varepsilon Z\).  If either endpoint
\(x=m+\theta\varepsilon Z\) or
\(x-\varepsilon Z=m-(1-\theta)\varepsilon Z\) lies in
\(N_{\ell_\varepsilon}(S)\), then
\[
 m\in N_{\ell_\varepsilon+R_J\varepsilon}(S).
\]
The additional condition \(x\in\operatorname{spt}\zeta\) keeps \(m\) in the fixed compact
set \(K\).  The volume of the displayed tubular set inside \(K\) is at most
\(C_S(\ell_\varepsilon+R_J\varepsilon)^2\).  Since \(W\) is bounded on \([0,1]\), the
potential difference is bounded by \(C\ell_\varepsilon^2/\varepsilon\).  For the interaction
part use \(|(a-b)^2-(c-d)^2|\le2\) for \(a,b,c,d\in[0,1]\) and
\(\sup_K\|J(x,\cdot)\|_1=M_K\).  Its absolute difference is at most
\[
 \frac C\varepsilon(\ell_\varepsilon+R_J\varepsilon)^2=o(1).
\]
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:poly}
If \(P\) is polyhedral in a neighbourhood of \(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\), then there are
\(u_\varepsilon:\mathbb R^d\to[0,1]\) with
\(u_\varepsilon\to\mathbf 1_P\) in \(L^1_{\rm loc}(\Omega)\) and
\[
 \limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_\varepsilon;\zeta)
 \le
 \int_{\partial P}\zeta(x)\gamma(x,\nu_P(x))
 \,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x).
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Fix \(\eta>0\).  Only finitely many faces of \(P\) meet \(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\).
If there are none, finite range gives
\(\mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(\mathbf 1_P;\zeta)=0\) for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\),
and there is nothing to prove.
Truncate them inside a compact polyhedral neighbourhood on whose outer
boundary \(\zeta=0\).  If \(N_F\) faces remain, apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:allocation} to each face \(F_i\), with phase normal \(n_i\),
using error \(\eta/N_F\).  This produces finitely many face
patches \(B_a\), profiles \(q_a\), and total allocated cost at most
\[
 \int_{\partial P}\zeta(x)\gamma(x,\nu_P(x))\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x)+\eta.
 \label{eq:allocated-total}
\]
Let \(S_\eta\) be the union of the original face junctions and all relative
patch boundaries.  It is a finite codimension-two polyhedral complex.

Let \(L\) exceed all transition radii of the finitely many \(q_a\)'s.  Finite
polyhedral geometry gives \(\kappa_\eta>0\) such that, away from
\(N_r(S_\eta)\), every point within distance \(\kappa_\eta r\) of
\(\partial P\) lies in a unique patch tube.  Set
\(\ell_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{2/3}\).  For all small \(\varepsilon\),
\[
 \varepsilon(2L+R_J)\le \frac{\kappa_\eta}{4}\ell_\varepsilon.
 \label{eq:separation}
\]
Outside \(N_{\ell_\varepsilon}(S_\eta)\), define in the tube of patch \(B_a\)
\[
 v_\varepsilon(x)=q_a\left(\frac{d_a(x)}\varepsilon\right),
\]
where \(d_a\) is signed distance to the supporting face, positive in \(P\).
Set \(v_\varepsilon=\mathbf 1_P\) away from all patch tubes.  Inside the collar choose any
measurable interpolation in \([0,1]\), for instance \(\mathbf 1_P\), and call the
result \(u_{\varepsilon,\eta}\).  The transition tubes have thickness \(O(\varepsilon)\),
while the collar has volume \(O_\eta(\ell_\varepsilon^2)\); hence
\(u_{\varepsilon,\eta}\to\mathbf 1_P\) locally in \(L^1\).

  Put \(C_\varepsilon=N_{\ell_\varepsilon}(S_\eta)\).  The proof of
  Lemma~\ref{lem:collar} gives, uniformly over all \([0,1]\)-valued choices in
  \(C_\varepsilon\),
  \[
   \frac{C_\eta}{\varepsilon}|N_{\ell_\varepsilon+R_J\varepsilon}(S_\eta)\cap K|
   \le \frac{C_\eta}{\varepsilon}(\ell_\varepsilon+R_J\varepsilon)^2=o(1).
  \]
  Hence all potential terms in \(C_\varepsilon\) and all interactions having at least
  one endpoint there may be removed at an \(o(1)\) cost.  For every patch set
  \[
   B_{a,\varepsilon}:=
   \{y\in B_a:\operatorname{dist}(y,\partial_F B_a)>2\ell_\varepsilon\}.
  \]
  Here \(\partial_F\) denotes relative boundary in the supporting face.  One
  has \(\mathcal H^{d-1}(B_a\setminus B_{a,\varepsilon})=O_\eta(\ell_\varepsilon)\).  Since the
  potential profile has compact support in \(s\), and the interaction profile
  is supported in \(|s|\le L+R_J\) with \(J\) uniformly bounded in
  \(L^1_Z\), the total cost over these deleted face strips is
  \(O_\eta(\ell_\varepsilon)=o(1)\).
  After deleting both the collar and these strips, condition
  \eqref{eq:separation} ensures that every remaining non-zero interaction has
  its two endpoint projections in one and the same safe patch.

  On the resulting safe patch, for the potential term write
  \(x=y+\varepsilon s n_i\); it
converges to
\[
 \int_{B_a}\zeta(y)\int_\mathbb R W(q_a(s))\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(y).
\]
For the interaction term first set \(m=x-\theta\varepsilon Z\), and then write
\(m=y+\varepsilon s n_i\).  Up to the explicitly estimated collar and face-strip
terms, the integral is
\begin{align*}
 \frac14\int_{B_a}\int_\mathbb R\int_{\mathbb R^d}
 &\zeta(y+\varepsilon s n_i+\theta\varepsilon Z)J(y+\varepsilon s n_i,Z)\\
 &\times|q_a(s+\theta Z\cdot n_i)
       -q_a(s-(1-\theta)Z\cdot n_i)|^2
 \,\mathrm d Z\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(y),
\end{align*}
where tangential shifts of the patch base are confined to the same removed
strip.  The difference factor vanishes unless \(|s|\le L+R_J\).  On the relevant compact set,
\(\|J(x,\cdot)\|_1\) is uniformly bounded, and
\[
 \sup_{|h|\le (L+R_J)\varepsilon}
 \|J(y+h,\cdot)-J(y,\cdot)\|_1\to0
\]
uniformly for \(y\) in the compact patch and \(|s|\le L+R_J\), by
\eqref{eq:l1-cont}.  Dominated convergence therefore gives the limit
\[
 \frac14\int_{B_a}\zeta(y)\int_\mathbb R\int_{\mathbb R^d}J(y,Z)
 |q_a(s)-q_a(s-Z\cdot n_i)|^2
 \,\mathrm d Z\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(y).
\]
Here, for each fixed \(Z\), the last identification uses the translation
\(s\mapsto s+\theta Z\cdot n_i\).
Summing over the finite allocation and using \eqref{eq:allocated-total} yields
\[
 \limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_{\varepsilon,\eta};\zeta)
 \le \int_{\partial P}\zeta\gamma(\cdot,\nu_P)\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}+\eta.
\]
Write the surface integral on the right as \(G_P\), choose
\(\eta_k\downarrow0\), and let \((K_m)\) exhaust \(\Omega\) by compact sets.
For each \(k\), choose \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\) so that, whenever
\(0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_k\),
\[
 \mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_{\varepsilon,\eta_k};\zeta)
      \le G_P+2\eta_k,
 \qquad
 \sum_{m=1}^k\|u_{\varepsilon,\eta_k}-\mathbf 1_P\|_{L^1(K_m)}\le k^{-1}.
\]
For \(\varepsilon\in(\varepsilon_{k+1},\varepsilon_k]\), set
\(u_\varepsilon=u_{\varepsilon,\eta_k}\).  Then \(u_\varepsilon\to\mathbf 1_P\) locally in
\(L^1\) and
\(\limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_\varepsilon;\zeta)\le G_P\).
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:strict}
Let \(E\) have finite perimeter in a neighbourhood of \(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\).  There
are measurable sets \(P_j\), polyhedral in a fixed neighbourhood of
\(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\), such that \(\mathbf 1_{P_j}\to\mathbf 1_E\) in
\(L^1_{\rm loc}(\Omega)\) and
\[
 \limsup_{j\to\infty}
 \int_{\partial P_j}\zeta(x)\gamma(x,\nu_{P_j}(x))\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x)
 \le
 \int_{\partial^*E}\zeta(x)\gamma(x,\nu_E(x))\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x).
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Choose open sets
\(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\Subset U\Subset V\Subset\Omega\) such that \(E\) has finite
perimeter in \(V\) and \(|D\mathbf 1_E|(\partial U)=0\).  Strict local
polyhedral approximation gives sets \(R_j\), polyhedral in \(U\), with
\[
 \mathbf 1_{R_j}\to\mathbf 1_E\text{ in }L^1(U),\qquad
 D\mathbf 1_{R_j}\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}D\mathbf 1_E,\qquad
 |D\mathbf 1_{R_j}|(U)\to|D\mathbf 1_E|(U)
\]
\citep{ambrosio1993polyhedral,ambrosio2000functions,maggi2012sets}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:cell-regularity} shows that the restriction of \(\Phi\) to
\(\overline U\times\mathbb S^{d-1}\) is bounded and upper semicontinuous.  Choose
bounded continuous functions \(\phi_k\) on this compact space such that
\(\phi_k\downarrow\Phi\) there, and define
\[
 \Phi_k(x,p):=
 \begin{cases}
  |p|\phi_k(x,p/|p|),&p\ne0,\\
  0,&p=0.
 \end{cases}
\]
Each \(\Phi_k\) is continuous on \(\overline U\times\mathbb R^d\), positively
one-homogeneous, and has linear growth.  Reshetnyak continuity for strict convergence of
vector measures gives, for every fixed \(k\),
\[
 \lim_{j\to\infty}
 \int_U\Phi_k\left(x,\frac{\,\mathrm d D\mathbf 1_{R_j}}{\,\mathrm d|D\mathbf 1_{R_j}|}\right)
 \,\mathrm d|D\mathbf 1_{R_j}|
 =
 \int_U\Phi_k\left(x,\frac{\,\mathrm d D\mathbf 1_E}{\,\mathrm d|D\mathbf 1_E|}\right)
 \,\mathrm d|D\mathbf 1_E|.
\]
Since \(\Phi\le\Phi_k\), first take the limsup in \(j\), then let
\(k\to\infty\).  Dominated convergence on the finite measure
\(|D\mathbf 1_E|\) yields
\[
 \limsup_{j\to\infty}
 \int_U\Phi\left(x,\frac{\,\mathrm d D\mathbf 1_{R_j}}{\,\mathrm d|D\mathbf 1_{R_j}|}\right)
 \,\mathrm d|D\mathbf 1_{R_j}|
 \le
 \int_U\Phi\left(x,\frac{\,\mathrm d D\mathbf 1_E}{\,\mathrm d|D\mathbf 1_E|}\right)
 \,\mathrm d|D\mathbf 1_E|.
\]
Set \(P_j=R_j\) in \(U\) and \(P_j=E\) outside \(U\).  Since
\(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\Subset U\), the splice has positive distance from
\(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\).  It has no weighted surface cost, and finite interaction range
ensures that the later diffuse recovery cannot sample it for all sufficiently
small \(\varepsilon\).  The asserted local convergence and inequality follow.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:diagonal}
Suppose \(P_j\to E\) locally in measure and
\[
 \limsup_{j\to\infty}G_j\le G,
 \qquad
 G_j:=\int_{\partial P_j}\zeta\gamma(\cdot,\nu_{P_j})\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}.
\]
If for every fixed \(j\) there are \(u_\varepsilon^j\to\mathbf 1_{P_j}\) locally in
\(L^1\) with
\(\limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_\varepsilon^j;\zeta)\le G_j\), then
there is one family \(u_\varepsilon\to\mathbf 1_E\) locally in \(L^1\) satisfying
\[
 \limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_\varepsilon;\zeta)\le G.
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
If \(G=+\infty\), take \(u_\varepsilon=\mathbf 1_E\).  Assume \(G<\infty\).  Let
\((K_m)\) be a compact exhaustion of \(\Omega\).  Pass to a subsequence, not
relabelled, for which every \(G_j\) is finite, \(G_j\le G+o(1)\), and
\[
 \sum_{m=1}^j
 \|\mathbf 1_{P_j}-\mathbf 1_E\|_{L^1(K_m)}\le j^{-1}.
\]
The last condition follows by a further diagonal extraction from the local
convergence \(P_j\to E\).  Choose \(\varepsilon_j\downarrow0\)
so that, whenever \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_j\),
\[
 \sum_{m=1}^j\|u_\varepsilon^j-\mathbf 1_{P_j}\|_{L^1(K_m)}\le j^{-1},
 \qquad
 \mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_\varepsilon^j;\zeta)\le G_j+j^{-1}.
\]
For \(\varepsilon\in(\varepsilon_{j+1},\varepsilon_j]\), set \(u_\varepsilon=u_\varepsilon^j\).  The two
assertions follow from the displayed approximation rate, the triangle
inequality, and the bound on \(G_j\).
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Choose \(P_j\) from Proposition~\ref{prop:strict}.  Proposition
\ref{prop:poly} supplies a recovery family for each fixed \(P_j\), and
Lemma~\ref{lem:diagonal} gives the required single family.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:compact-tail}
Let \(K\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)\) be non-negative, even, and supported in \(B_R\), and
let \(n\in\mathbb S^{d-1}\).  Suppose \(q:\mathbb R\to[0,1]\) has finite profile energy
\[
 E_{K,n}(q):=\int_\mathbb R W(q(s))\,\mathrm d s
 +\frac14\int_\mathbb R\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(Z)
 |q(s)-q(s-Z\cdot n)|^2\,\mathrm d Z\,\mathrm d s
\]
and satisfies \(q(s)\to0\) as \(s\to-\infty\) and
\(q(s)\to1\) as \(s\to+\infty\).  For \(L>R\), set
\[
 q_L(s):=
 \begin{cases}
  0,&s\le-L,\\
  q(s),&|s|<L,\\
  1,&s\ge L.
 \end{cases}
\]
Then \(q_L\in\mathcal A\) and \(E_{K,n}(q_L)\to E_{K,n}(q)\).
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The potential term converges because
\(\int W(q_L)=\int_{-L}^LW(q)\).  Put \(a=Z\cdot n\) and let
\(A_L(a)\) be the set of \(s\) for which at least one of \(s,s-a\) lies
outside \((-L,L)\).  On the complement of \(A_L(a)\), the increments of
\(q_L\) and \(q\) agree.  Moreover,
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R^d}K(Z)\int_{A_L(Z\cdot n)}
 |q(s)-q(s-Z\cdot n)|^2\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d Z\longrightarrow0
\]
by dominated convergence, since the full interaction density of \(q\) is
integrable.

Define
\[
 \alpha_L:=\sup_{s\ge L-R}|1-q(s)|
       +\sup_{s\le-L+R}|q(s)|.
\]
Then \(\alpha_L\to0\).  If the increment of \(q_L\) is non-zero on
\(A_L(a)\), the segment with endpoints \(s,s-a\) crosses one of
\(\{-L,L\}\).  The set of such \(s\) has measure at most \(2|a|\), and the
increment is bounded by \(\alpha_L\).  Consequently
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R^d}K(Z)\int_{A_L(Z\cdot n)}
 |q_L(s)-q_L(s-Z\cdot n)|^2\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d Z
 \le2\alpha_L^2\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(Z)|Z\cdot n|\,\mathrm d Z\longrightarrow0.
\]
The interaction energies therefore converge as claimed.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:frozen-tension}
Under \eqref{eq:uniform-core} and \eqref{eq:true-wells}, for every fixed
\(x_0\in\Omega\), the density \(n\mapsto\gamma(x_0,n)\) is the surface tension
of the homogeneous Kac functional with kernel \(J(x_0,\cdot)\).  Its
positively one-homogeneous extension is finite and convex; in particular,
\(\gamma(x_0,\cdot)\) is continuous on \(\mathbb S^{d-1}\).
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We first record the normalization needed to apply the homogeneous results.
Set \(v=2u-1\), \(\widetilde J=J(x_0,\cdot)/4\), and define
\[
 \widetilde W(v):=
 \begin{cases}
  W((v+1)/2),&|v|\le1,\\
  |v|-1,&|v|>1.
 \end{cases}
\]
This extension is continuous, has zeroes only at \(\{-1,1\}\), and has linear
growth.  Moreover, truncation to \([-1,1]\) does not increase either the
potential or the pair-interaction term.  Thus the unrestricted homogeneous
problem has the same infimum as its \([-1,1]\)-valued restriction.  On
functions valued in \([0,1]\),
the homogeneous energy for \((J(x_0,\cdot),W)\) is then exactly the energy for
\((\widetilde J,\widetilde W)\) after the affine change of variables, since
\[
 \frac14\widetilde J(Z)|v(x)-v(x-\varepsilon Z)|^2
 =\frac14J(x_0,Z)|u(x)-u(x-\varepsilon Z)|^2.
\]
Both sides use the ordered pair integral; restricting both endpoints to a set
and changing variables from the second endpoint to \(Z\) preserves the factor
\(1/4\).  The
kernel \(\widetilde J\) is non-negative, even, integrable, and has finite first
moment, so the hypotheses of the homogeneous theorem are satisfied.

The homogeneous optimal-profile theorem identifies the multidimensional
planar cell problem with its one-dimensional restriction
\citep{alberti1998optimal}.  That result is stated with profiles converging to
the wells at infinity.  Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-tail}, applied after the affine
phase change, shows that the infimum is unchanged when profiles are required
to equal the pure phases outside a compact interval.  Thus its cell value
agrees with \eqref{eq:cell}.  The homogeneous \(\Gamma\)-limit theorem identifies this
surface tension as a lower-semicontinuous anisotropic perimeter density
\citep{alberti1998nonlocal}.  Its one-homogeneous extension is consequently
convex.  Finiteness follows from the step-profile bound, and finite convex
one-homogeneous functions are continuous.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:liminf}
Assume \eqref{eq:uniform-core}, \eqref{eq:relative-continuity}, and
\eqref{eq:true-wells}.  Let
\(u_\varepsilon:\mathbb R^d\to[0,1]\) satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{\varepsilon>0}\mathcal K_{\varepsilon,A}^{J,\theta}(u_\varepsilon)<\infty
 \qquad\text{for every }A\Subset\Omega.
 \label{eq:local-bound}
\end{equation}
Then a subsequence converges in \(L^1_{\rm loc}(\Omega)\) to \(\mathbf 1_E\) for
some set \(E\) of locally finite perimeter.  Moreover, whenever the whole
sequence converges to \(\mathbf 1_E\), every \(\zeta\in C_c(\Omega)\),
\(\zeta\ge0\), satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
 \mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_\varepsilon;\zeta)
 \ge
 \int_{\partial^*E}\zeta(x)\gamma(x,\nu_E(x))\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x).
 \label{eq:liminf}
\end{equation}
Together with Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, this gives matching interior
sharp-interface bounds for this intrinsically coercive class.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
\emph{Step 1: compactness.}
Fix \(A'\Subset A\Subset\Omega\), and choose a compact \(K\) containing a
neighbourhood of \(\overline A\).  For all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), the
coefficient points associated with first endpoints in \(A\) belong to \(K\).
Set
\[
 J_{{\rm c},K}(Z):=j_K\mathbf 1_{B_{r_K}}(Z).
\]
Condition \eqref{eq:uniform-core} gives
\(J(x-\theta\varepsilon Z,Z)\ge J_{{\rm c},K}(Z)\) for \(x\in A\).  Hence
\(\mathcal K_{\varepsilon,A}^{J,\theta}\) controls the internal homogeneous energy
\[
 \frac1\varepsilon\int_A W(u_\varepsilon)\,\mathrm d x
 +\frac{j_K}{4\varepsilon}\int_A
   \int_{\substack{Z\in B_{r_K}\\x-\varepsilon Z\in A}}
   |u_\varepsilon(x)-u_\varepsilon(x-\varepsilon Z)|^2\,\mathrm d Z\,\mathrm d x.
\]
Indeed, one restricts the interaction to \(Z\in B_{r_K}\) and to pairs with
both endpoints in \(A\), and then discards all remaining non-negative terms.
The kernel \(J_{{\rm c},K}\) and
the true-well condition \eqref{eq:true-wells} satisfy the hypotheses of the
homogeneous compactness theorem on \(A'\), after the affine normalization used
in Lemma~\ref{lem:frozen-tension} \citep{alberti1998nonlocal}.  Since
\(A'\Subset A\), this is an interior application and produces no artificial
boundary contribution.  A diagonal
extraction on an exhaustion of \(\Omega\) gives
\(u_\varepsilon\to\mathbf 1_E\) in \(L^1_{\rm loc}\), with \(E\) of locally finite
perimeter.

\emph{Step 2: energy measures.}
It suffices to prove \eqref{eq:liminf} along a subsequence realizing its left
side.  On a relatively compact open set containing \(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\), define
positive Radon measures
\begin{align*}
 \mu_\varepsilon(B)
 &:=\frac1\varepsilon\int_B W(u_\varepsilon(x))\,\mathrm d x\\
 &\quad+\frac1{4\varepsilon}\int_B\int_{\mathbb R^d}
 J(x-\theta\varepsilon Z,Z)|u_\varepsilon(x)-u_\varepsilon(x-\varepsilon Z)|^2\,\mathrm d Z\,\mathrm d x.
\end{align*}
The local bound gives, after a further extraction,
\(\mu_\varepsilon\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}\mu\).  We prove
\begin{equation}
 \mu\ge
 \gamma(x,\nu_E(x))\mathcal H^{d-1}\mathbin{\vrule height 1.4ex depth -0.4ex
 width 0.07ex\vrule height 0.07ex depth -0.02ex width 0.7ex}\partial^*E.
 \label{eq:measure-domination}
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 3: multiplicative freezing.}
Fix \(x_0\in\partial^*E\), and let \(\rho_{x_0}\) and \(\omega_{x_0}\) be
supplied by \eqref{eq:relative-continuity}.  If
\(x\in B_r(x_0)\) and \(r+R_J\varepsilon\le\rho_{x_0}\), then
\begin{align*}
 J(x-\theta\varepsilon Z,Z)
 &\ge \bigl(1-\delta_{r,\varepsilon}\bigr)J(x_0,Z),
 \qquad
 \delta_{r,\varepsilon}:=\omega_{x_0}(r+R_J\varepsilon).
\end{align*}
Here we used
\(|x-\theta\varepsilon Z-x_0|\le r+R_J\varepsilon\).  Define the internal frozen energy
\begin{align}
 \mathcal K_\varepsilon^{x_0}(u;B_r(x_0))
 &:=\frac1\varepsilon\int_{B_r(x_0)}W(u(x))\,\mathrm d x \notag\\
 &\quad+\frac1{4\varepsilon}\int_{B_r(x_0)}
 \int_{\{Z:\,x-\varepsilon Z\in B_r(x_0)\}}J(x_0,Z)
 |u(x)-u(x-\varepsilon Z)|^2\,\mathrm d Z\,\mathrm d x.
 \label{eq:frozen-internal}
\end{align}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mu_\varepsilon(B_r(x_0))
 \ge(1-\delta_{r,\varepsilon})
 \mathcal K_\varepsilon^{x_0}(u_\varepsilon;B_r(x_0)),
 \label{eq:freeze}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the variable energy first controls the frozen energy with all second
endpoints, and dropping the cross-boundary interactions gives exactly
\eqref{eq:frozen-internal} and can only lower that energy.

\emph{Step 4: frozen liminf and differentiation.}
Choose radii \(r\downarrow0\) for which both \(\mu\) and
\(|D\mathbf 1_E|\) give zero mass to \(\partial B_r(x_0)\), and restrict to
\(r<\rho_{x_0}/2\).  For each fixed such \(r\), one has
\(\delta_{r,\varepsilon}\le\omega_{x_0}(2r)\) for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\).
Passing \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) in \eqref{eq:freeze} and applying the homogeneous
frozen liminf theorem on the ball gives
\begin{equation}
 \mu(B_r(x_0))
 \ge
 \bigl(1-\omega_{x_0}(2r)\bigr)
 \int_{\partial^*E\cap B_r(x_0)}
 \gamma(x_0,\nu_E(y))\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(y).
 \label{eq:ball-density}
\end{equation}
Indeed, by evenness of \(J(x_0,\cdot)\),
\eqref{eq:frozen-internal} is exactly the homogeneous pair-interaction
functional with both endpoints in \(B_r(x_0)\), written in the displacement
variable \(Z\).  The ball is a regular open set, and the affine normalization
in Lemma~\ref{lem:frozen-tension} puts the functional in the form of the
classical lower-bound theorem.
At \(|D\mathbf 1_E|\)-almost every reduced-boundary point, \(x_0\) is a
Lebesgue point of the polar field \(\nu_E\) relative to \(|D\mathbf 1_E|\).
Lemma~\ref{lem:frozen-tension} gives continuity of
\(n\mapsto\gamma(x_0,n)\).  Divide \eqref{eq:ball-density} by
\(|D\mathbf 1_E|(B_r(x_0))\) and let \(r\downarrow0\).  The differentiation
theorem for Radon measures yields
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d\mu}{\,\mathrm d|D\mathbf 1_E|}(x_0)
 \ge\gamma(x_0,\nu_E(x_0))
 \quad\text{for }|D\mathbf 1_E|\text{-a.e. }x_0,
\]
which is \eqref{eq:measure-domination}.

Finally, weak-star convergence of \(\mu_\varepsilon\) and continuity of \(\zeta\)
give
\[
 \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_\varepsilon;\zeta)
 =\int\zeta\,\mathrm d\mu
 \ge\int_{\partial^*E}\zeta(x)\gamma(x,\nu_E(x))\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x),
\]
along the selected subsequence, proving the liminf inequality.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
Fix \(A'\Subset A\Subset\Omega\), and choose a compact \(K\) containing a
neighbourhood of \(\overline A\).  For all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), the
coefficient points associated with first endpoints in \(A\) belong to \(K\).
Set
\[
 J_{{\rm c},K}(Z):=j_K\mathbf 1_{B_{r_K}}(Z).
\]
Condition \eqref{eq:uniform-core} gives
\(J(x-\theta\varepsilon Z,Z)\ge J_{{\rm c},K}(Z)\) for \(x\in A\).  Hence
\(\mathcal K_{\varepsilon,A}^{J,\theta}\) controls the internal homogeneous energy
\[
 \frac1\varepsilon\int_A W(u_\varepsilon)\,\mathrm d x
 +\frac{j_K}{4\varepsilon}\int_A
   \int_{\substack{Z\in B_{r_K}\\x-\varepsilon Z\in A}}
   |u_\varepsilon(x)-u_\varepsilon(x-\varepsilon Z)|^2\,\mathrm d Z\,\mathrm d x.
\]
Indeed, one restricts the interaction to \(Z\in B_{r_K}\) and to pairs with
both endpoints in \(A\), and then discards all remaining non-negative terms.
The kernel \(J_{{\rm c},K}\) and
the true-well condition \eqref{eq:true-wells} satisfy the hypotheses of the
homogeneous compactness theorem on \(A'\), after the affine normalization used
in Lemma~\ref{lem:frozen-tension} \citep{alberti1998nonlocal}.  Since
\(A'\Subset A\), this is an interior application and produces no artificial
boundary contribution.  A diagonal
extraction on an exhaustion of \(\Omega\) gives
\(u_\varepsilon\to\mathbf 1_E\) in \(L^1_{\rm loc}\), with \(E\) of locally finite
perimeter.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
It suffices to prove \eqref{eq:liminf} along a subsequence realizing its left
side.  On a relatively compact open set containing \(\operatorname{spt}\zeta\), define
positive Radon measures
\begin{align*}
 \mu_\varepsilon(B)
 &:=\frac1\varepsilon\int_B W(u_\varepsilon(x))\,\mathrm d x\\
 &\quad+\frac1{4\varepsilon}\int_B\int_{\mathbb R^d}
 J(x-\theta\varepsilon Z,Z)|u_\varepsilon(x)-u_\varepsilon(x-\varepsilon Z)|^2\,\mathrm d Z\,\mathrm d x.
\end{align*}
The local bound gives, after a further extraction,
\(\mu_\varepsilon\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}\mu\).  We prove
\begin{equation}
 \mu\ge
 \gamma(x,\nu_E(x))\mathcal H^{d-1}\mathbin{\vrule height 1.4ex depth -0.4ex
 width 0.07ex\vrule height 0.07ex depth -0.02ex width 0.7ex}\partial^*E.
 \label{eq:measure-domination}
\end{equation}
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- head-4: body_md -->
Fix \(x_0\in\partial^*E\), and let \(\rho_{x_0}\) and \(\omega_{x_0}\) be
supplied by \eqref{eq:relative-continuity}.  If
\(x\in B_r(x_0)\) and \(r+R_J\varepsilon\le\rho_{x_0}\), then
\begin{align*}
 J(x-\theta\varepsilon Z,Z)
 &\ge \bigl(1-\delta_{r,\varepsilon}\bigr)J(x_0,Z),
 \qquad
 \delta_{r,\varepsilon}:=\omega_{x_0}(r+R_J\varepsilon).
\end{align*}
Here we used
\(|x-\theta\varepsilon Z-x_0|\le r+R_J\varepsilon\).  Define the internal frozen energy
\begin{align}
 \mathcal K_\varepsilon^{x_0}(u;B_r(x_0))
 &:=\frac1\varepsilon\int_{B_r(x_0)}W(u(x))\,\mathrm d x \notag\\
 &\quad+\frac1{4\varepsilon}\int_{B_r(x_0)}
 \int_{\{Z:\,x-\varepsilon Z\in B_r(x_0)\}}J(x_0,Z)
 |u(x)-u(x-\varepsilon Z)|^2\,\mathrm d Z\,\mathrm d x.
 \label{eq:frozen-internal}
\end{align}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mu_\varepsilon(B_r(x_0))
 \ge(1-\delta_{r,\varepsilon})
 \mathcal K_\varepsilon^{x_0}(u_\varepsilon;B_r(x_0)),
 \label{eq:freeze}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the variable energy first controls the frozen energy with all second
endpoints, and dropping the cross-boundary interactions gives exactly
\eqref{eq:frozen-internal} and can only lower that energy.
<!-- end head-4 -->
<!-- head-5: body_md -->
Choose radii \(r\downarrow0\) for which both \(\mu\) and
\(|D\mathbf 1_E|\) give zero mass to \(\partial B_r(x_0)\), and restrict to
\(r<\rho_{x_0}/2\).  For each fixed such \(r\), one has
\(\delta_{r,\varepsilon}\le\omega_{x_0}(2r)\) for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\).
Passing \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) in \eqref{eq:freeze} and applying the homogeneous
frozen liminf theorem on the ball gives
\begin{equation}
 \mu(B_r(x_0))
 \ge
 \bigl(1-\omega_{x_0}(2r)\bigr)
 \int_{\partial^*E\cap B_r(x_0)}
 \gamma(x_0,\nu_E(y))\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(y).
 \label{eq:ball-density}
\end{equation}
Indeed, by evenness of \(J(x_0,\cdot)\),
\eqref{eq:frozen-internal} is exactly the homogeneous pair-interaction
functional with both endpoints in \(B_r(x_0)\), written in the displacement
variable \(Z\).  The ball is a regular open set, and the affine normalization
in Lemma~\ref{lem:frozen-tension} puts the functional in the form of the
classical lower-bound theorem.
At \(|D\mathbf 1_E|\)-almost every reduced-boundary point, \(x_0\) is a
Lebesgue point of the polar field \(\nu_E\) relative to \(|D\mathbf 1_E|\).
Lemma~\ref{lem:frozen-tension} gives continuity of
\(n\mapsto\gamma(x_0,n)\).  Divide \eqref{eq:ball-density} by
\(|D\mathbf 1_E|(B_r(x_0))\) and let \(r\downarrow0\).  The differentiation
theorem for Radon measures yields
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d\mu}{\,\mathrm d|D\mathbf 1_E|}(x_0)
 \ge\gamma(x_0,\nu_E(x_0))
 \quad\text{for }|D\mathbf 1_E|\text{-a.e. }x_0,
\]
which is \eqref{eq:measure-domination}.
<!-- end head-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:pointwise-gamma}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:liminf}, every
\(u_\varepsilon\to\mathbf 1_E\) in \(L^1_{\rm loc}(\Omega)\) satisfies
\[
 \liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal K_\varepsilon^{J,\theta}(u_\varepsilon;\zeta)
 \ge \int_{\partial^*E}\zeta(x)\gamma(x,\nu_E(x))
 \,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x).
\]
Together with Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, this identifies the pointwise
\(\Gamma\)-limit at every finite-perimeter characteristic state.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:ray-measure-cell-formula}
Let \(\mu\) be a finite, non-negative Borel measure on \(\mathbb R^d\) with compact
support and finite first moment, and let \(M\ge\mu(\mathbb R^d)\).  For the profile
problem obtained from \eqref{eq:profile-cost} by replacing
\(J(Z)\,\mathrm d Z\) with \(\mu(\,\mathrm d Z)\), the steep potential \(W_M=M d_*\) gives
the exact one-homogeneous cell density
\begin{equation}
 h_\mu(\xi)=\frac14\int_{\mathbb R^d}|Z\cdot\xi|\mu(\,\mathrm d Z).
 \label{eq:measure-kernel-cell}
\end{equation}
In particular, \eqref{eq:ray-radial-law}--\eqref{eq:ray-measure} give
\begin{equation}
 h_\nu(\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^N c_i|v_i\cdot\xi|.
 \label{eq:zonotope-density}
\end{equation}
This is a norm if and only if \(\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_N\}=\mathbb R^d\).
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The threshold map \(\chi(r)=\mathbf 1_{\{r\ge1/2\}}\) satisfies
\eqref{eq:diffuse-rounding-pointwise}.  Integrating that inequality first in
the profile variable and then against \(\mu\) gives
\[
 e_\mu(n;\chi\circ q)-e_\mu(n;q)
 \le\bigl(\mu(\mathbb R^d)-M\bigr)
       \int_\mathbb R d_*(q(r))\,\mathrm d r\le0.
\]
Thus it is enough to minimize over binary profiles.  For every
\(v:\mathbb R\to\{0,1\}\) with the prescribed end states and every \(s\in\mathbb R\),
truncate on \((-R,R)\), count the net transition, and let \(R\to\infty\) to
obtain
\[
 \int_\mathbb R|v(r)-v(r-s)|\,\mathrm d r\ge |s|.
\]
The monotone step attains equality for every \(s\) simultaneously.  Since
binary squared differences equal absolute differences, integration against
\(\mu\) proves \eqref{eq:measure-kernel-cell}.  Substituting
\eqref{eq:ray-measure} and using \(\int t\,\mathrm d\lambda=1\) yields
\[
 \frac14\,2\sum_i c_i\int_a^b
 \bigl(|t v_i\cdot\xi|+|-t v_i\cdot\xi|\bigr)\lambda(\,\mathrm d t)
 =\sum_i c_i|v_i\cdot\xi|.
\]
The last expression vanishes precisely on the orthogonal complement of the
span of the \(v_i\), which proves the norm criterion.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:ray-measure-gamma-limit}
Assume \eqref{eq:ray-radial-law}, \(M\ge m_\nu\), and
\(\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_N\}=\mathbb R^d\).  In the strong
\(L^1(\mathbb T^d)\) topology, the functionals
\(\mathcal F_\varepsilon^\nu\) Gamma-converge as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) to
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal F_0^\nu(u):=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\int_{\partial^*E}h_\nu(\nu_E)\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1},
   &u=\mathbf 1_E,\quad E\text{ of finite perimeter in }\mathbb T^d,\\[4pt]
 +\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{eq:ray-gamma-limit}
\end{equation}
The family is equicoercive in \(L^1\).  More precisely:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item if \(u_\varepsilon\to u\) in \(L^1\), then
 \(\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal F_\varepsilon^\nu(u_\varepsilon)
 \ge\mathcal F_0^\nu(u)\);
 \item for every finite-perimeter set \(E\), the constant binary sequence
 \(u_\varepsilon=\mathbf 1_E\) is a recovery sequence.
\end{enumerate}
The lower bound and recovery remain valid for any finite radial measure with
unit first moment.  The density bounds in \eqref{eq:ray-radial-law} are used
only for equicoercivity.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
We separate rounding, the directional lower bound, recovery, and compactness.
For a periodic field \(u\), translation invariance and
\eqref{eq:diffuse-rounding-pointwise} give
\begin{align}
 \mathcal F_\varepsilon^\nu(\chi\circ u)-\mathcal F_\varepsilon^\nu(u)
 &\le \frac{m_\nu-M}{\varepsilon}
       \int_{\mathbb T^d}d_*(u)\,\mathrm d x\le0.
 \label{eq:ray-global-rounding}
\end{align}
Moreover
\begin{equation}
 \|u-\chi\circ u\|_{L^1}=\int_{\mathbb T^d}d_*(u)\,\mathrm d x
 \le\frac\varepsilon M\mathcal F_\varepsilon^\nu(u).
 \label{eq:ray-rounding-distance}
\end{equation}
Hence any bounded-energy sequence may be replaced by a binary sequence
\(z_\varepsilon\) without increasing its energy or changing its \(L^1\) limit.
For binary fields, \eqref{eq:ray-measure} reduces the energy exactly to
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal F_\varepsilon^\nu(z)
 =\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{c_i}{\varepsilon}
   \int_a^b\int_{\mathbb T^d}
   |z(x)-z(x-\varepsilon t v_i)|\,\mathrm d x\lambda(\,\mathrm d t).
 \label{eq:ray-binary-directional-energy}
\end{equation}

Suppose first that \(z_\varepsilon\to z\) in \(L^1\).  For fixed \(t>0\), the
difference quotients converge distributionally:
\[
 \frac{z_\varepsilon(\,cdot+\varepsilon t v_i)-z_\varepsilon}{\varepsilon t}
 \longrightarrow D_{v_i}z.
\]
Indeed, testing against \(\phi\in C^1(\mathbb T^d)\), changing variables,
and using uniform convergence of the corresponding difference quotient of
\(\phi\) proves the assertion.  Lower semicontinuity of total variation then
gives
\begin{equation}
 |D_{v_i}z|(\mathbb T^d)
 \le\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\frac1{\varepsilon t}
 \int_{\mathbb T^d}|z_\varepsilon(x)-z_\varepsilon(x-\varepsilon t v_i)|\,\mathrm d x.
 \label{eq:ray-directional-liminf}
\end{equation}
Fatou's lemma, followed by \(\int t\,\mathrm d\lambda=1\), yields from
\eqref{eq:ray-binary-directional-energy}
\[
 \liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal F_\varepsilon^\nu(z_\varepsilon)
 \ge\sum_i c_i|D_{v_i}z|(\mathbb T^d).
\]
If the left side is finite, \eqref{eq:ray-rounding-distance} makes \(z\)
binary.  Since the \(v_i\) span \(\mathbb R^d\), finite variation in these
directions implies \(z\in BV\), and the polar decomposition of \(Dz\) gives
\[
 \sum_i c_i|D_{v_i}z|
 =\int_{\mathbb T^d}\sum_i c_i|v_i\cdot\sigma_z|\,\mathrm d|Dz|
 =\int_{\partial^*E}h_\nu(\nu_E)\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}
\]
when \(z=\mathbf 1_E\).  This proves the Gamma-liminf.

For recovery, let \(z=\mathbf 1_E\in BV(\mathbb T^d;\{0,1\})\).  The standard
translation characterization of directional variation gives, for every
fixed \(t\in(a,b)\),
\begin{equation}
 \frac1\varepsilon\int_{\mathbb T^d}
 |z(x)-z(x-\varepsilon t v_i)|\,\mathrm d x
 \longrightarrow t|D_{v_i}z|(\mathbb T^d).
 \label{eq:ray-translation-limit}
\end{equation}
The BV translation estimate bounds the left side by
\(t|D_{v_i}z|(\mathbb T^d)\).  Dominated convergence in \(t\), the unit
first moment of \(\lambda\), and \eqref{eq:ray-binary-directional-energy}
therefore prove
\(\mathcal F_\varepsilon^\nu(\mathbf 1_E)\to\mathcal F_0^\nu(\mathbf 1_E)\).

It remains to justify equicoercivity, because averaging only at finitely many
single shifts would not suffice.  Choose a basis
\(v_{i_1},\ldots,v_{i_d}\) from the given directions.  For a binary bounded
energy sequence \(z_\varepsilon\), \eqref{eq:ray-radial-law} and
\eqref{eq:ray-binary-directional-energy} imply
\begin{equation}
 \int_a^b\frac1\varepsilon
 \|z_\varepsilon(\cdot-\varepsilon t v_{i_j})-z_\varepsilon\|_{L^1}\,\mathrm d t\le C
 \quad(j=1,\ldots,d).
 \label{eq:ray-averaged-translation-bound}
\end{equation}
Divide \((a,b)\) into three equal subintervals.  In the first and third one,
select \(a_{j,\varepsilon}<b_{j,\varepsilon}\), respectively, so that each selected shift
has \(L^1\) difference at most \(C\varepsilon\); their separation is bounded below
by \((b-a)/3\).  Let \(S_{j,\varepsilon}\) average translations along \(v_{i_j}\)
over \([\varepsilon a_{j,\varepsilon},\varepsilon b_{j,\varepsilon}]\).  Then
\begin{align}
 \|S_{j,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon-z_\varepsilon\|_{L^1}&\le C\varepsilon,
 \label{eq:ray-smoothing-distance}\\
 |D_{v_{i_j}}S_{j,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon|(\mathbb T^d)
 &\le\frac{
 \|z_\varepsilon(\cdot-\varepsilon b_{j,\varepsilon}v_{i_j})
      -z_\varepsilon(\cdot-\varepsilon a_{j,\varepsilon}v_{i_j})\|_{L^1}}
 {\varepsilon(b_{j,\varepsilon}-a_{j,\varepsilon})}\le C.
 \label{eq:ray-smoothing-variation}
\end{align}
The numerator in the last line is bounded by the two selected translation
differences.  The averaging operators commute and are \(L^1\) contractions.
Thus \(Z_\varepsilon:=S_{1,\varepsilon}\cdots S_{d,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon\) is uniformly bounded in
\(BV\), while \(\|Z_\varepsilon-z_\varepsilon\|_1\to0\).  BV compactness and
\eqref{eq:ray-rounding-distance} prove equicoercivity for the original
sequence.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:heterogeneous-fixed-ray-gamma}
Assume \eqref{eq:ray-radial-law},
\eqref{eq:heterogeneous-fixed-ray-assumptions}, and
\(\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_N\}=\mathbb R^d\).  Then
\(\mathcal F_\varepsilon^{c,v}\) is equicoercive and Gamma-converges in strong
\(L^1(\mathbb T^d)\) to
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal F_0^{c,v}(u):=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\int_{\partial^*E}h_{c,v}(x,\nu_E(x))\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x),
 &u=\mathbf 1_E,\ E\text{ of finite perimeter},\\[4pt]
 +\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{eq:heterogeneous-fixed-ray-limit}
\end{equation}
Every finite-perimeter set has the constant binary recovery sequence
\(u_\varepsilon=\mathbf 1_E\).  In particular, no polyhedral approximation is needed.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The pointwise rounding estimate \eqref{eq:diffuse-rounding-pointwise} and the
symmetry of every bond give
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal F_\varepsilon^{c,v}(\chi\circ u)-\mathcal F_\varepsilon^{c,v}(u)
 \le\frac{4\Lambda Nc^*-M}{\varepsilon}\int d_*(u)\,\mathrm d x\le0.
 \label{eq:heterogeneous-fixed-rounding}
\end{equation}
Also \(\|u-\chi\circ u\|_1\le(\varepsilon/M)\mathcal F_\varepsilon^{c,v}(u)\).
It is therefore enough to consider binary fields \(z_\varepsilon\).

Fix \(i\) and \(t\).  The measures
\begin{equation}
 \mu_{i,\varepsilon,t}:=
 \frac{z_\varepsilon-z_\varepsilon(\,\cdot-\varepsilon t v_i)}{\varepsilon t}\,\mathcal L^d
 \stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}D_{v_i}z
 \label{eq:heterogeneous-directional-measure-convergence}
\end{equation}
distributionally whenever \(z_\varepsilon\to z\) in \(L^1\).  Since
\(a_{i,\varepsilon,t}\to c_i\) uniformly, weighted lower semicontinuity of total
variation yields
\begin{equation}
 \int c_i\,\mathrm d|D_{v_i}z|
 \le\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int a_{i,\varepsilon,t}\,\mathrm d|\mu_{i,\varepsilon,t}|.
 \label{eq:heterogeneous-weighted-directional-liminf}
\end{equation}
Fatou in \(t\), followed by \(\int t\,\mathrm d\lambda=1\), proves the liminf.
The lower bound \(a_{i,\varepsilon,t}\ge c_*\), applied to a fixed basis among the
\(v_i\), reduces equicoercivity to the smoothing argument in
\eqref{eq:ray-averaged-translation-bound}--\eqref{eq:ray-smoothing-variation}.

For \(z=\mathbf 1_E\), the weighted translation formula for BV functions gives
\begin{equation}
 \frac1\varepsilon\int c_i(x)|z(x)-z(x-\varepsilon t v_i)|\,\mathrm d x
 \longrightarrow t\int c_i\,\mathrm d|D_{v_i}z|.
 \label{eq:heterogeneous-weighted-translation-limit}
\end{equation}
The BV translation estimate and the bounds on \(c_i\) provide an integrable
majorant in \(t\).  Moreover endpoint freezing is quantitative:
\begin{align}
 &\left|\frac1\varepsilon\int
 [a_{i,\varepsilon,t}(x)-c_i(x)]|z(x)-z(x-\varepsilon t v_i)|\,\mathrm d x\right|
 \notag\\
 &\hspace{25mm}\le
 \frac\varepsilon2\|\nabla c_i\|_\infty t^2|v_i|\,|D_{v_i}z|(\mathbb T^d).
 \label{eq:heterogeneous-endpoint-freezing-error}
\end{align}
Dominated convergence proves recovery and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:ordered-flow-local-coordinates}
There are \(r_0,\delta_0,C_0>0\), depending only on \(d,N,\kappa,c^*\)
and the norms in \eqref{eq:flow-ray-regularity}, with the following property.
For every \(x_0\) one can select an ordered \(d\)-tuple
\(I=(i_1,\ldots,i_d)\) and define
\begin{equation}
 \Theta_{x_0,I}(s)
 :=\Phi_{i_d}^{s_d}\circ\cdots\circ\Phi_{i_1}^{s_1}(x_0),
 \qquad s\in Q_{r_0}:=(-r_0,r_0)^d,
 \label{eq:ordered-flow-chart}
\end{equation}
so that \(\Theta_{x_0,I}\) is bi-Lipschitz onto its image.  Writing
\(J_{x_0,I}:=|\det D_s\Theta_{x_0,I}|\), one has
\begin{align}
 \delta_0|s-s'|&\le
 |\Theta_{x_0,I}(s)-\Theta_{x_0,I}(s')|
 \le C_0|s-s'|,                                      \label{eq:flow-chart-bilip}\\
 \Theta_{x_0,I}(s)&=x_0+\sum_{k=1}^ds_kv_{i_k}(x_0)+R_{x_0,I}(s),
 \notag\\[-2pt]
 |R(s)-R(s')|&\le C_0r_0|s-s'|,                    \label{eq:flow-chart-linearization}\\
 \bigl|J_{x_0,I}(s)-|\det V_I(x_0)|\bigr|&\le C_0|s|,
 \qquad 0<\delta_0\le J_{x_0,I}\le C_0 .          \label{eq:flow-chart-jacobian}
\end{align}
Moreover, interchanging two adjacent flows changes the chart by at most
\begin{equation}
 \left|\Phi_j^t\Phi_i^s(x)-\Phi_i^s\Phi_j^t(x)\right|
 \le C_0|st|,
 \qquad |s|+|t|\le r_0.
 \label{eq:flow-chart-commutator-error}
\end{equation}
The torus admits a finite cover by smaller images of such charts, with a
Lipschitz partition of unity subordinate to the cover.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Put \(A(x)\xi=(\sqrt{c_i(x)}v_i(x)\cdot\xi)_{i=1}^N\).
Condition \eqref{eq:flow-ray-spanning} and \(c_i\le c^*\) imply
\begin{equation}
 \|A(x)\xi\|_{\ell^2}
 \ge \kappa_0|\xi|,
 \qquad \kappa_0:=\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{Nc^*}},
 \label{eq:ordered-frame-singular-value}
\end{equation}
because \(\sum_i c_i|v_i\cdot\xi|
\le\sqrt{Nc^*}\,\|A(x)\xi\|_{\ell^2}\).
Consequently \(\det(A^{\mathsf T}A)\ge\kappa_0^{2d}\).  Cauchy--Binet and
\(c_i\le c^*\) then give, at every \(x\), a minor
\(V_I(x)=(v_{i_1}(x),\ldots,v_{i_d}(x))\) satisfying
\begin{equation}
 |\det V_I(x)|\ge
 \delta_1:=\frac{\kappa_0^d}
 {\sqrt{\binom Nd}\,(c^*)^{d/2}}>0.
 \label{eq:ordered-frame-minor-bound}
\end{equation}
Since the fields are
Lipschitz, Gronwall's inequality gives
\begin{equation}
 |\Phi_i^s(x)-x-sv_i(x)|\le C s^2,
 \qquad \operatorname{Lip}(\Phi_i^s-\mathrm{Id})\le C|s|.
 \label{eq:single-flow-linearization}
\end{equation}
Iterating \eqref{eq:single-flow-linearization} yields
\eqref{eq:flow-chart-linearization}.  Choose \(r_0\) so that its Lipschitz
remainder is at most half the least singular value of every selected
\(V_I(x_0)\).  The quantitative Lipschitz inverse theorem gives
\eqref{eq:flow-chart-bilip}.  More explicitly, differentiating the ordered
composition in \(s_k\) gives the \(k\)-th column
\begin{equation}
 D_{s_k}\Theta_{x_0,I}(s)
 =D\Phi_{i_d}^{s_d}\cdots D\Phi_{i_{k+1}}^{s_{k+1}}
   v_{i_k}(x_k),
 \label{eq:ordered-chart-column-formula}
\end{equation}
where \(x_k=\Phi_{i_k}^{s_k}\circ\cdots\circ
\Phi_{i_1}^{s_1}(x_0)\).  The flow variational equation and the Lipschitz
bounds give
\(\|D_s\Theta_{x_0,I}(s)-V_I(x_0)\|\le C|s|\).
The determinant Lipschitz estimate on bounded matrices, together with
\eqref{eq:ordered-frame-minor-bound}, yields the frozen-Jacobian estimate and,
after reducing \(r_0\) once more, the two positive Jacobian bounds in
\eqref{eq:flow-chart-jacobian}.  These identities hold for the
\(C^{1,1}\) representatives furnished by \(W^{2,\infty}\); no smooth
approximation of the vector fields is needed.  Finally, two applications of
\eqref{eq:single-flow-linearization} give
\eqref{eq:flow-chart-commutator-error}.  Compactness of \(\mathbb T^d\)
produces the finite cover.  Notice that no Frobenius condition was used.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:ordered-flow-smoothing}
Let \(z_\varepsilon:\mathbb T^d\to\{0,1\}\) satisfy
\begin{equation}
 B_\varepsilon:=\sum_i\int_a^b\frac1\varepsilon\int
 |z_\varepsilon-z_\varepsilon\circ\Phi_i^{-\varepsilon t}|\,\mathrm d x\lambda(\,\mathrm d t)\le C.
 \label{eq:flow-ray-averaged-bound}
\end{equation}
For \(0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_{\rm sm}\), there are
\(Z_\varepsilon\in BV(\mathbb T^d)\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \|Z_\varepsilon-z_\varepsilon\|_{L^1}\le C_{\rm sm}\varepsilon B_\varepsilon,
 \qquad |DZ_\varepsilon|(\mathbb T^d)\le C_{\rm sm} B_\varepsilon.
 \label{eq:ordered-flow-smoothing-bound}
\end{equation}
The constant is independent of \(\varepsilon\) and \(z_\varepsilon\), and its dependence
on all analytic and atlas data is displayed in
\eqref{eq:ordered-flow-constant-data}--
\eqref{eq:ordered-flow-explicit-constant}.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
We use parameter-space integration by parts, which avoids differentiating an
unsmoothed field through a chain of noncommuting averages.

\emph{Step 1: signed increments supplied by the radial interval.}
For one field put
\(d_{i,\varepsilon}(s):=\|z_\varepsilon-z_\varepsilon\circ\Phi_i^{-\varepsilon s}\|_1\).
The group property, the triangle inequality, and the Liouville bound give
\begin{align}
 \int_\mathbb R k_\rho(s)d_{i,\varepsilon}(s)\,\mathrm d s
 &=\iint\rho(t)\rho(r)d_{i,\varepsilon}(t-r)\,\mathrm d t\,\mathrm d r\notag\\
 &\le C e^{2\varepsilon_0bD_0}
   \int_a^b\rho(t)d_{i,\varepsilon}(t)\,\mathrm d t .
 \label{eq:ordered-signed-increment}
\end{align}
Indeed, insert the intermediate state
\(z_\varepsilon\circ\Phi_i^{\varepsilon r}\), then change variables once in each term.
Since \(k_\rho\ge k_*\) on the support of \(\eta\) and \(\eta'\),
\begin{equation}
 \int_{-c_\rho}^{c_\rho}(\eta+|\eta'|)(s)
 d_{i,\varepsilon}(s)\,\mathrm d s
 \le C\varepsilon R_\rho B_\varepsilon,
 \label{eq:ordered-signed-source}
\end{equation}
where the lower bound for \(w\) converts \(\rho\,\mathrm d t\) to
\(\lambda(\,\mathrm d t)\).

\emph{Step 2: a full-dimensional ordered parameter kernel.}
For the selected frame \(I_\alpha=(i_{\alpha,1},\ldots,i_{\alpha,d})\), set
\begin{align}
 T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s)
 &:={\Phi}_{i_{\alpha,d}}^{-\varepsilon s_d}\circ\cdots\circ
 {\Phi}_{i_{\alpha,1}}^{-\varepsilon s_1}(x),\notag\\
 \eta_d(s)&:=\prod_{k=1}^d\eta(s_k),\qquad
 A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\eta_d(s)
 z(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s))\,\mathrm d s .
 \label{eq:ordered-flow-average}
\end{align}
For \(x\in U_\alpha^-\), every point in this formula lies in
\(U_\alpha^+\).  Write
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s):=D_xT_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s),\qquad
 \mathsf B_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s):=-\varepsilon^{-1}D_sT_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s).
 \label{eq:ordered-parameter-matrices}
\end{equation}
Put \(x_0=x\) and
\(x_k=\Phi_{i_{\alpha,k}}^{-\varepsilon s_k}(x_{k-1})\).  If
\begin{equation}
 R_k:=D\Phi_{i_{\alpha,d}}^{-\varepsilon s_d}(x_{d-1})\cdots
 D\Phi_{i_{\alpha,k+1}}^{-\varepsilon s_{k+1}}(x_k),
 \qquad R_d=I,
 \label{eq:ordered-later-flow-product}
\end{equation}
then the chain rule gives the exact column formula
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf B_{\alpha,\varepsilon}e_k
 =R_kv_{i_{\alpha,k}}(x_k),
 \qquad
 \mathsf A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}
 =D\Phi_{i_{\alpha,d}}^{-\varepsilon s_d}(x_{d-1})\cdots
  D\Phi_{i_{\alpha,1}}^{-\varepsilon s_1}(x_0).
 \label{eq:ordered-parameter-columns}
\end{equation}
In particular \(\mathsf B_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,0)=V_{I_\alpha}(x)\) and
\(\mathsf A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,0)=I\).

The first and second variational equations for a \(C^{1,1}\) flow give,
for \(|r|\le\varepsilon c_\rho\),
\begin{align}
 \|D\Phi_i^r\|&\le e^{|r|V_1},\notag\\
 \|D\Phi_i^r-I\|&\le e^{|r|V_1}-1,\notag\\
 \|D^2\Phi_i^r\|&\le |r|V_2e^{3|r|V_1}.
 \label{eq:ordered-flow-first-second-variation}
\end{align}
Indeed, differentiate \(\dot\Phi_i^r=v_i(\Phi_i^r)\) once and twice in the
initial point and apply Gronwall.  Since
\(|x_k-x|\le d\varepsilon c_\rho V_0e^{d\varepsilon c_\rho V_1}\),
\eqref{eq:ordered-parameter-columns} yields
\begin{align}
 \|\mathsf A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}-I\|
 &\le e^{d\varepsilon c_\rho V_1}-1,\notag\\
 \|\mathsf B_{\alpha,\varepsilon}-V_{I_\alpha}(x)\|
 &\le C_d\varepsilon c_\rho V_0V_1e^{2d\varepsilon c_\rho V_1}.
 \label{eq:ordered-parameter-freezing}
\end{align}
The definition of \(\varepsilon_{\rm sm}\) and the Neumann-series estimate therefore
give
\begin{equation}
 \|\mathsf A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\|+\|\mathsf B_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\|
 +\|\mathsf B_{\alpha,\varepsilon}^{-1}\|
 \le C_d(1+K_{\rm fr})e^{2d\varepsilon_0c_\rho V_1}.
 \label{eq:ordered-parameter-inverse-bound}
\end{equation}
Differentiating \eqref{eq:ordered-parameter-columns} in one parameter and
using \eqref{eq:ordered-flow-first-second-variation} gives, term by term,
\begin{equation}
 \|\nabla_s\mathsf A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\|+
 \|\nabla_s\mathsf B_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\|
 \le C_d\varepsilon(1+V_0)(V_1+V_2)
 e^{C_d d\varepsilon_0c_\rho V_1}.
 \label{eq:ordered-parameter-matrix-bounds}
\end{equation}
Thus, for each Euclidean basis vector \(e_\ell\),
\begin{equation}
 a_{\alpha,\ell}:=\mathsf B_{\alpha,\varepsilon}^{-1}
 \mathsf A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}e_\ell .
 \end{equation}
 It satisfies
 \begin{equation}
 \|a_{\alpha,\ell}\|_{L^\infty_s}
 +\|\nabla_sa_{\alpha,\ell}\|_{L^\infty_s}
 \le C_d(1+K_{\rm fr})^2(1+V_0)(1+V_1+V_2)
 e^{C_d d\varepsilon_0c_\rho V_1}.
 \label{eq:ordered-parameter-coefficients}
\end{equation}

For smooth \(z\), the identity
\[
 \nabla z(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon})\mathsf A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}e_\ell
 =-\varepsilon^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^d
 a_{\alpha,\ell k}\,\partial_{s_k}
 z(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon})
\]
and integration by parts in the compact parameter cube give
\begin{equation}
 \partial_\ell A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z(x)
 =\frac1\varepsilon\sum_{k=1}^d\int
 \partial_{s_k}(\eta_d a_{\alpha,\ell k})(x,s)
 [z(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s))-z(x)]\,\mathrm d s .
 \label{eq:ordered-parameter-integration-by-parts}
\end{equation}
The subtraction is exact because the integral of every parameter derivative
vanishes.  It is the step that removes all derivatives of \(z\).

Let \(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}^{(0)}(x,s)=x\) and let
\(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}^{(j)}\) be the composition of the first \(j\) factors in
\eqref{eq:ordered-flow-average}.  The exact telescoping identity is
\begin{equation}
 z(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s))-z(x)
 =\sum_{j=1}^d
 \left[z(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}^{(j)}(x,s))
       -z(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}^{(j-1)}(x,s))\right].
 \label{eq:ordered-path-telescoping}
\end{equation}
Changing variables by \(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}^{(j-1)}\), whose inverse Jacobian is
at most \(e^{d\varepsilon c_\rho D_0}\), gives
\begin{equation}
 \int_{U_\alpha^-}|z(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s))-z(x)|\,\mathrm d x
 \le e^{d\varepsilon c_\rho D_0}
 \sum_{j=1}^dd_{i_{\alpha,j},\varepsilon}(s_j).
 \label{eq:ordered-telescoping-jacobian}
\end{equation}
Moreover \eqref{eq:ordered-parameter-coefficients} implies
\begin{equation}
 |\partial_{s_k}(\eta_da_{\alpha,\ell k})|
 \le C_{\rm par}(|\eta'(s_k)|+\eta(s_k))
       \prod_{j\ne k}\eta(s_j),
 \label{eq:ordered-parameter-weight-bound}
\end{equation}
where
\[
 C_{\rm par}:=C_d(1+K_{\rm fr})^2(1+V_0)(1+V_1+V_2)
 e^{C_d d\varepsilon_0b(V_1+D_0)}.
\]
Insert \eqref{eq:ordered-telescoping-jacobian} first with weight \(\eta_d\)
and then with each weight in
\eqref{eq:ordered-parameter-weight-bound}.  Fubini and
\eqref{eq:ordered-signed-source} give, without an unlisted remainder,
\begin{align}
 \|A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon-z_\varepsilon\|_{L^1(U_\alpha^-)}
 &\le d e^{d\varepsilon c_\rho D_0} C\varepsilon R_\rho B_\varepsilon,
 \label{eq:localized-ordered-flow-distance}\\
 |D(A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon)|(U_\alpha^-)
 &\le d^2C_{\rm par}e^{d\varepsilon c_\rho D_0}CR_\rho B_\varepsilon.
 \label{eq:localized-ordered-flow-variation}
\end{align}
Equivalently, the whole parameter system closes in the single estimate
\begin{equation}
 |D(A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon)|(U_\alpha^-)
 +\varepsilon^{-1}\|A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon-z_\varepsilon\|_{L^1(U_\alpha^-)}
 \le C B_\varepsilon.
 \label{eq:ordered-smoothing-coupled-absorption}
\end{equation}
There is no first-cycle derivative and no commutator remainder to absorb.
For general \(z_\varepsilon\in L^1\), convolve it temporarily in the physical
variable.  The right-hand sides converge by continuity of composition with a
bi-Lipschitz flow, while the averaged fields converge in \(L^1\).  Lower
semicontinuity of variation passes the two estimates to \(z_\varepsilon\).

The \(W^{2,\infty}\) regularity in
\eqref{eq:flow-ray-regularity} is used precisely in
\eqref{eq:ordered-flow-first-second-variation} and nowhere else in the
compactness argument.  Approximation is needed only for the scalar field
\(z\); all constants remain those displayed above.

\emph{Step 3: gluing.}
Choose \(\chi_\alpha\in C_c^1(U_\alpha^-)\),
\(\sum_\alpha\chi_\alpha=1\), and put
\begin{equation}
 Z_\varepsilon:=\sum_\alpha\chi_\alpha
 A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon .
 \label{eq:localized-flow-gluing}
\end{equation}
Since
\begin{align}
 DZ_\varepsilon={}&\sum_\alpha\chi_\alpha
 D(A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon)
 +\sum_\alpha(A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon-z_\varepsilon)D\chi_\alpha,
 \label{eq:partition-cancellation-identity}
\end{align}
the finite overlap, \eqref{eq:localized-ordered-flow-distance}, and
\eqref{eq:localized-ordered-flow-variation} give
\eqref{eq:ordered-flow-smoothing-bound} with \(C_{\rm sm}\).
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- head-6: body_md -->
For one field put
\(d_{i,\varepsilon}(s):=\|z_\varepsilon-z_\varepsilon\circ\Phi_i^{-\varepsilon s}\|_1\).
The group property, the triangle inequality, and the Liouville bound give
\begin{align}
 \int_\mathbb R k_\rho(s)d_{i,\varepsilon}(s)\,\mathrm d s
 &=\iint\rho(t)\rho(r)d_{i,\varepsilon}(t-r)\,\mathrm d t\,\mathrm d r\notag\\
 &\le C e^{2\varepsilon_0bD_0}
   \int_a^b\rho(t)d_{i,\varepsilon}(t)\,\mathrm d t .
 \label{eq:ordered-signed-increment}
\end{align}
Indeed, insert the intermediate state
\(z_\varepsilon\circ\Phi_i^{\varepsilon r}\), then change variables once in each term.
Since \(k_\rho\ge k_*\) on the support of \(\eta\) and \(\eta'\),
\begin{equation}
 \int_{-c_\rho}^{c_\rho}(\eta+|\eta'|)(s)
 d_{i,\varepsilon}(s)\,\mathrm d s
 \le C\varepsilon R_\rho B_\varepsilon,
 \label{eq:ordered-signed-source}
\end{equation}
where the lower bound for \(w\) converts \(\rho\,\mathrm d t\) to
\(\lambda(\,\mathrm d t)\).
<!-- end head-6 -->
<!-- head-7: body_md -->

\begin{align}
 T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s)
 &:={\Phi}_{i_{\alpha,d}}^{-\varepsilon s_d}\circ\cdots\circ
 {\Phi}_{i_{\alpha,1}}^{-\varepsilon s_1}(x),\notag\\
 \eta_d(s)&:=\prod_{k=1}^d\eta(s_k),\qquad
 A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\eta_d(s)
 z(T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s))\,\mathrm d s .
 \label{eq:ordered-flow-average}
\end{align}
For \(x\in U_\alpha^-\), every point in this formula lies in
\(U_\alpha^+\).  Write
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s):=D_xT_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s),\qquad
 \mathsf B_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s):=-\varepsilon^{-1}D_sT_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,s).
 \label{eq:ordered-parameter-matrices}
\end{equation}
Put \(x_0=x\) and
\(x_k=\Phi_{i_{\alpha,k}}^{-\varepsilon s_k}(x_{k-1})\).  If
\begin{equation}
 R_k:=D\Phi_{i_{\alpha,d}}^{-\varepsilon s_d}(x_{d-1})\cdots
 D\Phi_{i_{\alpha,k+1}}^{-\varepsilon s_{k+1}}(x_k),
 \qquad R_d=I,
 \label{eq:ordered-later-flow-product}
\end{equation}
then the chain rule gives the exact column formula
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf B_{\alpha,\varepsilon}e_k
 =R_kv_{i_{\alpha,k}}(x_k),
 \qquad
 \mathsf A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}
 =D\Phi_{i_{\alpha,d}}^{-\varepsilon s_d}(x_{d-1})\cdots
  D\Phi_{i_{\alpha,1}}^{-\varepsilon s_1}(x_0).
 \label{eq:ordered-parameter-columns}
\end{equation}
In particular \(\mathsf B_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,0)=V_{I_\alpha}(x)\) and
\(\mathsf A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(x,0)=I\).
<!-- end head-7 -->
<!-- head-8: body_md -->
Choose \(\chi_\alpha\in C_c^1(U_\alpha^-)\),
\(\sum_\alpha\chi_\alpha=1\), and put
\begin{equation}
 Z_\varepsilon:=\sum_\alpha\chi_\alpha
 A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon .
 \label{eq:localized-flow-gluing}
\end{equation}
Since
\begin{align}
 DZ_\varepsilon={}&\sum_\alpha\chi_\alpha
 D(A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon)
 +\sum_\alpha(A_{\alpha,\varepsilon}z_\varepsilon-z_\varepsilon)D\chi_\alpha,
 \label{eq:partition-cancellation-identity}
\end{align}
the finite overlap, \eqref{eq:localized-ordered-flow-distance}, and
